articles.title: Facção proíbe venda de água mineral em Fortaleza e cidades do Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Para além da situação de Banabuiú, denúncias de falta de água mineral após ameaças de facção criminosa a comerciantes se espalharam por mais cidades do Ceará.
articles.summary: Ameaças de facção interrompem a venda de água mineral no Ceará, forçando moradores a usar fontes impróprias ou buscar galões sob escolta policial.
articles.body:
Ameaças da facção criminosa Comando Vermelho contra comerciantes já têm afetado o abastecimento de água mineral em bairros de Fortaleza e municípios do interior do Ceará. O cenário veio à tona após moradores de Banabuiú , no sertão central do Ceará, precisarem de escolta policial para comprar garrafões de água.

Depois que o g1 e a TV Verdes Mares noticiaram a situação em Banabuiú, moradores de outras localidades passaram a denunciar casos semelhantes onde moravam. Foram relatados casos em Bairros de Fortaleza , além das cidades de Meruoca e Caridade - esta última cidade, inclusive, é a mesma que, em 2025, ficou sem internet por ataques de facção.

Na capital cearense, as denúncias se concentram nos bairros Parque Dois Irmãos, Passaré e Manuel Dias Branco . A situação ocorreria, principalmente, em comunidades apontadas como áreas de atuação da facção.

Moradores de Banabuiú, no Ceará, recebem garrafões de água sob escolta policial após ameaça de facção — Foto: TV Verdes Mares/Reprodução

A primeira denúncia anônima relata a situação na Comunidade Rosalina, no Bairro Parque Dois Irmãos, em Fortaleza. Segundo a testemunha, a extorsão teria começado na última segunda-feira (2), feriado de Finados.

Criminosos estariam cobrando uma taxa de comerciantes para permitir o funcionamento de pontos de venda de água.

“Isso começou no dia 2 de novembro. Veio uma ordem do Rio de Janeiro para que começassem a cobrar pelo abastecimento de água mineral, aquelas águas de garrafão de 20 litros. O abastecimento já acabou lá no bairro. Ontem mesmo [acabou o produto] em cinco lugares. No sexto depósito foi que eu encontrei, e o rapaz falou que já estava acabando. E ele estava com medo de ir buscar lá na distribuidora”, relatou a testemunha, que será mantida em anonimato.

Denúncias de falta de água mineral após ameaças de facção criminosa a comerciantes se espalharam por mais cidades do Ceará. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Verdes Mares

Na cidade de Meruoca, a cerca de 250 quilômetros de Fortaleza, testemunhas afirmam que, diante das ameaças constantes de criminosos ao comércio local, moradores passaram a buscar água em poços e chafarizes.

Segundo os relatos, essa água não é potável nem adequada para consumo sem tratamento. Para beber, a população precisa ferver o líquido.

“As pessoas estão sem água. Está sendo proibida a venda de garrafão de água. Então as pessoas estão sobrevivendo pegando água no poço e até pagando para as pessoas pegarem no chafariz, porque foi proibida água em garrafões", diz o morador.

"E quem sofre são os moradores. A gente tem medo de falar por medo de represália. Essa é a situação. Quem não tem poço vai para o chafariz. Às vezes, no chafariz falta água e bebe do açude mesmo. E a água é imprópria, né? Fica até doente” , continua a testemunha.

A situação também estaria se repetindo em Caridade, município a cerca de 97 quilômetros de Fortaleza. Segundo as denúncias, moradores da cidade enfrentam dificuldade para ter acesso à água mineral, como ocorre em Banabuiú.

Caridade, inclusive, é o mesmo município que, em março de 2025, ficou quase totalmente sem internet após ataques de uma facção criminosa contra provedores de internet. Na ocasião, os criminosos romperam os fios das empresas, afetando 90% dos clientes da cidade.

A TV Verdes Mare s questinou a Secretaria da Segurança Pública e Defesa Social (SSPDS) sobre as denúncias, mas não obteve resposta até a última atualização desta reportagem.

articles.summary: Ukraine's national police on Wednesday released bodycam footage showing the moments before and after Russian bomb strikes hit an underground shelter in
articles.body: Ukraine's national police on Wednesday released bodycam footage showing the moments before and after Russian bomb strikes hit an underground shelter in the southern village of Kamyshuvakha, killing at least 40 people.The attack took place on Monday as residents had gathered at a former school and a nearby shelter to collect humanitarian aid.The footage, recorded by a police officer who was among those killed, shows the extensive damage caused by the first strike, with residents standing amid the rubble. A military official is then heard warning police officers over a two-way radio that more guided bombs were being launched towards the village."Quickly (go) to the shelter!" one of the officers is heard telling residents as they make their way into an underground shelter at least two floors below ground.Seconds later, an explosion is heard and flames are seen as another bomb strikes the shelter, bringing the recording to an abrupt end.Ukraine said nine guided bombs, some weighing up to 3,000 kg, struck the village in the Zaporizhzhia region, which lies near the front line. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said more than 30 people could still be trapped under the rubble as rescue operations continued for a third day. The death toll had risen to 40, making it one of the deadliest attacks in the region in nearly five years of war.Meanwhile, Russian attacks on Wednesday triggered power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions, disrupting supplies for several hours. Residents in the capital were urged to use public drinking water fountains until services were restored. Emergency centres were set up in the worst-affected areas, providing hot tea and facilities to charge electronic devices.Russia launched 310 drones overnight, including 81 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine's air force. In its daily social media update, the air force said 272 drones of various types had been downed or suppressed.Such aerial attacks have become a regular feature of life in Ukraine during the war. In 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for two senior Russian officers whom prosecutors accused of overseeing attacks on civilian infrastructure.Meanwhile, officials from the United States, Germany, France, Britain, NATO, the World Bank and the European Union met at the European Commission headquarters in Brussels on Wednesday to discuss the large-scale reconstruction effort that will be needed once the war ends.The latest attacks came after the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's southwestern Kherson region. The truce, the most significant between Kyiv and Moscow since 2022, had allowed residents to be evacuated from the devastated city.In Moscow, the Kremlin expressed hope that US President Donald Trump would continue his efforts to end the war in Ukraine regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections, which saw Democrats take control of Congress. articles.title: US midterms: Trump's veto powers & how he can use them to block Democrats' agenda
articles.summary: The Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections has dramatically reshaped the balance of power in Washington, handing the party sizeable
articles.body: The Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections has dramatically reshaped the balance of power in Washington, handing the party sizeable majorities in both chambers of Congress and setting the stage for a confrontation with President Donald Trump. With Republicans suffering a stunning electoral setback, Democrats are preparing to push an ambitious legislative agenda, reverse some of Trump's policies and launch investigations into his administration.However, their electoral gains do not mean they will have a free hand in passing laws. Trump retains one of the most significant constitutional weapons available to a US president: the power to veto legislation. The president has already signalled that he is prepared to use it, posting a photograph of a red baseball cap bearing the word "VETO" on Truth Social as the scale of the Democratic victory became apparent.“It’s the power of veto. It’s one of the stronger powers that a president has,” Trump said after the rout.Trump has also warned that he does not want to spend the next two years blocking everything Congress sends his way. "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything," he told Politico. Nevertheless, with Democrats preparing to challenge his policies, the veto could become a central instrument in the political battle between the White House and Capitol Hill.How Trump's veto power worksThe presidential veto is a constitutional safeguard designed to maintain a balance of power between the executive and legislative branches. Under Article I, Section 7 of the US Constitution, every bill passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate must be presented to the president before it can become law.The president has 10 days, excluding Sundays, to sign the legislation, return it unsigned with objections or allow it to become law. If Trump issues a regular veto, the bill goes back to the chamber where it originated, accompanied by his objections.Congress can still turn the legislation into law by overriding the veto, but this requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This is a significantly higher threshold than the simple majority generally required to pass legislation.Democrats' expanded majorities will give them considerable room to push bills through Congress, but they will remain short of the two-thirds support needed to override Trump's vetoes. Historically, Congress has overturned only a small proportion of presidential vetoes, making the power an effective legislative roadblock.Pocket veto: Trump's other weaponTrump also has another option: the pocket veto. Under this provision, if the president does not sign a bill within the 10-day period and Congress adjourns during that time, the legislation automatically fails to become law.Unlike a regular veto, a pocket veto cannot be overridden by Congress. Lawmakers would instead have to reintroduce the legislation, pass it through both chambers and send it to the president again.This gives the White House another way to block legislation, particularly when Congress is approaching an adjournment.Veto threats can shape legislation tooTrump does not necessarily have to wait for a bill to reach his desk to exercise influence. A presidential veto threat can pressure lawmakers into modifying legislation before it is passed.The White House can also communicate its position through Statements of Administration Policy (SAPs), which outline the administration's support or opposition to proposed legislation. These statements can include explicit warnings that the president intends to veto a bill.Meanwhile, Democrats have other ways to challenge Trump even without successfully passing legislation. They can use their congressional majorities to conduct investigations, summon administration officials, issue subpoenas and scrutinise government spending and policies.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Yaqub, Yassira and Shubham, three Pune schoolchildren who qualified for the Sarabhai Younglings Internship after succeeding in a national science aptitude test
articles.summary: For Yaqub Bangi, Yassira Memon and Shubham Pariyar, science has moved beyond school textbooks.
articles.body: For Yaqub Bangi, Yassira Memon and Shubham Pariyar, science has moved beyond school textbooks. The three students from Pune have earned places in the Sarabhai Younglings Internship 2026 after clearing both rounds of the national SPOT science aptitude test conducted by the Vikram Sarabhai Science Foundation.Their selection gives them an opportunity to learn about science and technology through exposure to leading institutions, including ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation. The programme's learning journey also includes the Indian Space Research Organisation's ISTRAC centre, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the India Meteorological Department and IIM Bangalore.Yaqub and Yassira study at K.C. Thackeray Vidya Niketan, while Shubham attends Epiphany High School. All three are part of the Scholars programme run by Panaah Communities, a Pune-based nonprofit that works with children and young people from low-income neighbourhoods. Their achievement is not just about qualifying for an internship. It also reflects what can happen when students receive consistent academic support and opportunities to explore subjects beyond their regular classrooms.From a classroom test to a national science opportunityThe three students qualified for the internship by clearing both stages of SPOT, which stands for Science Promotion Orient Test. Conducted annually by the Vikram Sarabhai Science Foundation, the assessment identifies students with an aptitude for science and encourages them to develop their understanding of the subject. The foundation describes SPOT as more than an examination. Its process is designed to encourage students to ask questions, gather information, test ideas and apply what they learn. Shortlisted students can access science-learning resources, interact with experts and take part in educational experiences.The Sarabhai Younglings programme offers selected students exposure to scientific work and institutions. The 2026 batch brought together students from different parts of India. Updates shared by the foundation also describe interactions with scientists and learning sessions on subjects such as satellite technology and weather forecasting. For Yaqub, Yassira and Shubham, this kind of exposure can help connect lessons learnt at school with the work being done in research, space science and technology.The support system behind the achievementAll three students are Scholars at Panaah Communities, an organisation that works within Pune's high-need neighbourhoods. Founded in 2021, Panaah aims to support children through their school years and help young people move towards higher education and employment. Its approach begins with a simple idea: academic difficulties should be addressed before they become reasons for a child to leave school. The organisation works with children in their own neighbourhoods through learning centres and mentors who understand the communities they serve.Panaah's work is organised around three stages: Solvers, Scholars and Professionals. Solvers supports children who are falling behind in foundational subjects such as reading and mathematics. Scholars work with students who show strong academic potential and prepare them for challenging examinations and learning opportunities. Professionals support older students as they move from school and college towards careers.Yaqub, Yassira and Shubham are part of the Scholars programme, which focuses on helping students strengthen their academic abilities and compete in national-level opportunities. The programme's progress is also reflected in its assessment data. According to Panaah, students in its Scholars group improved their performance on the Ei ASSET diagnostic assessment during the 2025-26 academic year. They moved from performing better than roughly one in four students nationally at the beginning of the year to doing better than around four in ten by its end.Why early support can make a differencePanaah's model is shaped by a concern that school dropout often begins long before a student reaches the secondary stage. When children struggle with reading or mathematics in the middle grades, the learning gap can grow over time. Eventually, keeping up with lessons becomes difficult, affecting their confidence and interest in school. The organisation therefore starts working with children as early as Grade 4 through its Solvers programme. Its mentors help students strengthen basic skills, while community-based projects encourage them to apply what they learn to everyday problems.For students who show a strong interest in academics, the Scholars programme creates another route. It provides additional guidance and helps them prepare for science and mathematics competitions, Olympiads and other opportunities. Panaah's co-founder and executive director, Shoeb Sayed, has described the organisation's approach as a continuous pathway, beginning with children who need help catching up and extending to young adults preparing for well-paying jobs. The idea is to build opportunities within the communities rather than expecting children to find them on their own.The selection of Yaqub, Yassira and Shubham shows one outcome of that approach. Three students from Pune's underserved neighbourhoods have cleared a national science assessment and earned a place in a programme that connects classroom learning with the wider world of science. Their journey is also a reminder that talent is not limited by a student's neighbourhood or family circumstances. With sustained guidance and access to opportunities, curiosity can become the starting point for much bigger possibilities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Maryland man sentenced to 5 years after creating fake charities linked to veterans, breast cancer and childhood leukaemia and stealing over $200,000
articles.summary: A Maryland man has been sentenced to five years in prison for creating fake charities and stealing more than $200,000 from people who believed they were
articles.body: A Maryland man has been sentenced to five years in prison for creating fake charities and stealing more than $200,000 from people who believed they were making charitable donations. James Trankle, 55, received a 60-month sentence for conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud, along with five counts of bank fraud.Between 2013 and 2018, he and a co-defendant solicited donations for organisations claiming to support disabled and paralyzed veterans, breast cancer awareness and children with leukaemia. They then used donors’ banking details to produce counterfeit cheques. A jury found Trankle guilty, and the court ordered him to pay $204,561 in restitution and forfeit $135,327.According to the US Department of Justice, many of the people targeted by the scheme were older adults. The defendants registered the fake organisations with the D.C. Department of Consumer and Regulatory Affairs and opened several bank accounts in their names.Maryland man created fake charities linked to veterans and cancer supportTrankle and his co-defendant, Stephen Sibert, created the fake charities between 2013 and 2018. They registered the entities with the D.C. Department of Consumer and Regulatory Affairs to make them appear legitimate. These included the Disabled and Paralyzed Veterans Fund, the National Breast Cancer Awareness Fund and the Children’s Leukemia of America Fund.Trankle used a post office box in Washington, D.C., as the official mailing address for the organisations. He also opened several bank accounts in their names. The pair then mailed donation requests to thousands of potential donors across the country, asking them to send personal cheques. They obtained more than 1,600 cheques from people who believed they were contributing to charitable causes.How did the Maryland man steal over $200,000 from charitable donorsTrankle deposited the personal cheques into bank accounts controlled by him and Sibert. An analysis of these accounts showed that the pair collected more than $45,000 from people who believed they were donating to legitimate organisations.The scheme also involved copying the bank account and routing information printed on donors’ cheques. Trankle and Sibert used these details to create additional counterfeit cheques without the account holders’ permission. The cheques were made payable to their fake charities and drawn against the donors’ personal current accounts.The pair deposited these counterfeit cheques into accounts they controlled before withdrawing and spending the money on personal expenses. They deposited more than 700 counterfeit cheques worth a combined total of over $150,000.Fake charity scheme targeted donors supporting veterans and cancer causesThe organisations did not carry out the charitable activities described in their donation requests. They also did not give significant amounts of money to other charities that could have supported these causes.Trankle concealed the scheme while operating a church from his office in Maryland. The US Postal Inspection Service’s Washington Division investigated the case.A jury found Trankle guilty on May 15, 2023, following a trial in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. His conviction arose from the scheme involving fake charitable organisations, donation requests and the misuse of donors’ banking information. The victims had believed their money would support charitable causes, but the funds were instead deposited into accounts controlled by the defendants.Court sentences Maryland man for fraud involving fake veterans and cancer charitiesUS Attorney Matthew M. Graves and Inspector-in-Charge Damon Wood of the US Postal Inspection Service’s Washington Division announced the sentence. US District Judge Trevor N. McFadden ordered Trankle to serve 60 months in prison, followed by five years of supervised release.The judge also ordered him to pay $204,561 in restitution and forfeit $135,327. These orders followed his conviction for conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud and five additional counts of bank fraud.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information. The information is based on the US Department of Justice's announcement of James Trankle's sentencing and should not be interpreted as independent confirmation.You use AI every day. articles.title: British couple met an abandoned girl in South Africa and turned a £10 fundraising challenge into a charity that has raised £29 million
articles.summary: A chance encounter with an abandoned child in South Africa changed the course of Phil and Wendy Wall's lives.
articles.body: A chance encounter with an abandoned child in South Africa changed the course of Phil and Wendy Wall's lives. During a visit in 1997, the British couple met a young girl named Zodwa, whose mother had left her behind. They tried to adopt her but could not make it happen. Instead, they began looking for a way to help other children in similar circumstances. Their first idea was an unusual fundraising challenge: give supporters £10 and ask them to turn it into £100 using their own skills and connections. That small experiment raised more than £2 million and eventually grew into WeSeeHope, a charity that says it has raised £29 million for vulnerable children.Meeting an abandoned girl in South Africa inspired the couple to actPhil and Wendy Wall were visiting South Africa in 1997 when they encountered Zodwa, a young girl who had been abandoned by her mother. The experience stayed with them, particularly after their attempt to adopt her proved unsuccessful. They realised that helping one child would not address the wider difficulties facing children across the region. At the time, the HIV and AIDS crisis had left large numbers of children orphaned or vulnerable in Southern and Eastern Africa. The couple began considering how they could support more families and communities, rather than focusing on a single case. Their eventual response was to build a fundraising initiative that anyone could take part in.Supporters received £10 and were challenged to raise £100The Walls came up with the 10¹⁰ Challenge, an idea built around a simple request: give someone £10 and see if they can turn it into £100. Instead of asking participants to make another donation, they encouraged them to put their own abilities, interests and contacts to work. People could decide how to grow the initial amount, making the campaign as much about individual initiative as fundraising. Phil and Wendy also put their personal savings into getting the project started. The challenge eventually brought in more than £2 million, giving the couple the resources and momentum to establish a permanent organisation, according to WeSeeHope's account of its beginnings.The fundraising initiative became a charity supporting children across AfricaIn 2000, Phil and Wendy formally established the organisation under the name HOPEHIV. Its initial work focused on children affected by the HIV and AIDS crisis in Southern and Eastern Africa. As its programmes developed, the charity expanded its geographical reach and approach. Its project office moved from South Africa to Tanzania in 2008, reflecting its growing work in Eastern Africa. In 2014, it introduced the Village Investors Programme, which helped communities establish savings and loans groups. The organisation adopted its present name, WeSeeHope, in 2015. What began as a fundraising response to one encounter had developed into a broader effort to help children and families build more secure futures.WeSeeHope reports raising £29 million for vulnerable childrenWeSeeHope says it has raised £29 million since its establishment, supporting vulnerable children and communities across Sub-Saharan Africa. Its programmes cover areas including education, entrepreneurship and household financial security. The Village Investors Programme, for example, had established 749 savings and loans groups by 2018, reaching more than 17,000 members and 46,000 children. The work also brought recognition for the couple behind the organisation. Phil and Wendy Wall received MBEs in the 2022 New Year Honours List for services to vulnerable children in Southern and Eastern Africa. In 2025, WeSeeHope marked 25 years since its formal establishment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: For people living along the coastlines of the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan, extreme weather is a familiar reality. However, the past few months have brought an unusually severe spell of storms, with their intensity and unpredictable movements causing widespread devastation.A series of powerful weather systems, intensified by the El Niño phenomenon, has claimed dozens of lives, disrupted air travel, damaged infrastructure and destroyed crops across large parts of East Asia.According to BBC, in October, Taiwan virtually came to a standstill as an enormous storm approached its north-eastern coastline. The typhoon, large enough to cover the island of 23 million people, generated winds of up to 295 kmph (193 mph), comparable to those of a Category 5 hurricane. Its strength was sufficient to destroy houses and generate powerful, potentially destructive waves.However, the storm did not make landfall in Taiwan, passing close to the island while bringing heavy rainfall. Despite avoiding a direct hit, it caused significant disruption across the region. Hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, coastal highways were closed as enormous waves battered the shoreline, while around 15,000 households in Japan's southern Okinawa islands experienced power outages.A succession of powerful stormsEl Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon associated with unusually warm ocean waters in the eastern Pacific and changes in atmospheric circulation. These conditions can influence weather patterns worldwide, increasing the likelihood of extreme weather events.The phenomenon typically occurs every two to seven years and can last for approximately a year. The current episode, which the UK met office has described as potentially the strongest in living memory, is expected to continue until February or March.The region has already experienced several major storms in recent months. In June, Japan faced the simultaneous approach of Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos towards its eastern coastline, prompting evacuation orders for nearly one million people.The following month, tropical storm Narra moved close to China's southern coastline near Guangxi, inundating villages and forcing tens of thousands of residents to leave their homes.In August, super typhoon dolphin travelled across the Pacific for 16 days before striking eastern China, triggering severe flooding and causing dozens of casualties. Later that month, Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three cities in south-eastern China within a week, disrupting transport services and prompting thousands to evacuate.Pacific Ocean generating greater storm intensityAccording to the accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) index, which measures the combined intensity of tropical cyclones during a season, the Pacific Ocean has accumulated substantial energy as a result of record-high temperatures linked to El Niño.The ACE reading for South-East and East Asia is projected to reach almost twice its 30-year average this year.Changes in wind patterns associated with El Niño are also influencing where typhoons develop. Storms are increasingly forming further east than usual and have more time to gather strength while travelling over unusually warm ocean waters.Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau, compared the pacific ocean to a person "burning with fever", warning at a Manila press briefing in September that it could soon experience severe disturbances.The outlook remains concerning. In October, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial pacific, monitored by the Japan meteorological agency for its El Niño forecasts, reached 4 degrees Celsius above normal. This was the highest level recorded since observations began in 1949. The previous record was 3.6 degrees celsius, registered in December 1997.China's climate agency has also cautioned that ocean temperatures could continue increasing over the following three months because of El Niño.Although the typhoon season generally reaches its peak between September and October, the continued warming of ocean waters has raised concerns that the region could face further destructive storms after enduring repeated weather emergencies.Scientists warn of escalating climate risksIn August, typhoon chan-hom surprised weather observers in Japan by travelling across the country from east to west, rather than following the more common south-to-north route.Japan's extensive disaster preparedness systems and well-equipped authorities enabled a swift evacuation response. However, countries with fewer resources and weaker emergency infrastructure could struggle to respond effectively to similarly unpredictable storms.To assess how rising temperatures could worsen extreme weather, manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and her research team simulated the potential effects of warmer conditions on some of the Philippines' most destructive storms. Their analysis included super typhoon Haiyan, also known as Yolanda, which struck in 2013 and killed more than 6,000 people.The researchers arrived at what Delfino described as "very, very scary findings". Their simulations indicated that higher temperatures could increase total accumulated rainfall by 26%.Such an increase could have devastating consequences for the Philippines, where flooding caused by monsoon rains and approximately 20 tropical storms annually remains a major natural disaster threat.In recent years, severe flooding has brought entire cities to a standstill for several days. Growing frustration over repeated flood-related disasters has also prompted Filipinos to protest against alleged corruption, which they claim has diverted millions of dollars allocated for flood-control infrastructure.In an article published on the university of the Philippines website, Delfino stressed the importance of ensuring that political leaders and government officials develop a stronger understanding of climate-related risks to improve community preparedness.Governments step up disaster preparednessGovernments across the region are taking measures to reduce the immediate impact of increasingly severe storms.Japan has advised residents to maintain supplies of food and essential items during the typhoon season. People have also been urged to secure outdoor furniture and other objects that could turn into dangerous projectiles during powerful winds.China, meanwhile, has instructed local authorities to identify vulnerable areas and strengthen weather monitoring and early-warning systems.The Philippines and other South-East Asian countries are also preparing for potential disruptions to agricultural production, particularly rice cultivation. Governments have expanded assistance to farmers, including the distribution of fertilisers, to minimise the impact on food supplies.However, the longer-term challenges remain uncertain. The united nations development programme (UNDP) in Asia and the Pacific has warned that the opportunity for governments to take preventive action against El Niño-related risks is narrowing.The organisation highlighted that the severity of an El Niño's impact on communities is often determined years before the phenomenon occurs. Factors such as the location of roads and settlements, water management systems, the reach of social protection programmes and the availability of emergency funds all influence how effectively communities can withstand extreme weather."Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," the UNDP said, underlining the need for sustained investment in disaster preparedness and climate resilienceYou use AI every day. articles.title: King cobras struggle to move freely through Thailand’s agricultural landscapes, with researchers identifying forest fragments and canal-side vegetation as important habitat
articles.summary: Farmland, roads and new settlements are spreading across the world, and wildlife is left to find its way through landscapes that people have reshaped.
articles.body: Farmland, roads and new settlements are spreading across the world, and wildlife is left to find its way through landscapes that people have reshaped. In northeastern Thailand, a study of king cobras, among the largest venomous snakes on Earth, shows what that looks like up close. Seven cobras tracked at the Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve moved less in agricultural areas and leaned on patches of natural vegetation, especially along irrigation canals. Broken-up landscapes, it seems, can hold animals back even when they live right beside people.Why are king cobras moving less through agricultural landscapes in ThailandAccording to the study published in Movement Ecology, titled ‘No room to roam: King Cobras reduce movement in agriculture, ’ researchers conducted the work in Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve, Nakhon Ratchasima province, northeastern Thailand. The landscape includes a protected forest core, a buffer zone being reforested, and a transitional zone used for rice, corn, and sugar cane. That farmed zone also holds 159 villages and a four-lane highway linking Nakhon Ratchasima to Bangkok, so wildlife habitat sits right next to farming and transport infrastructure.Seven king cobras were tracked between 22 March 2014 and 28 July 2018, with their locations logged around four times a day. Radio transmitters were implanted while the snakes were under anaesthesia, and positions were worked out by triangulation. The team tried to keep at least 10 metres away from the animals as they tracked them. Movement generally rose in forested areas but tended to fall in agricultural landscapes.Why do king cobras rely on natural vegetation in farmlandCobras crossing farmland kept their movements to vegetated semi-natural areas. These were scrub and vegetation that was not actively farmed, often found along field margins, irrigation canals and disused plots. The researchers singled these areas out as important because they gave the snakes routes through farmland where suitable natural habitat had been broken up.Not every snake reacted to the landscape in the same way. Some individuals were linked with semi-natural vegetation, while others showed different patterns around roads, settlements and other features. The researchers also noted that vegetation and water may offer cover and potential prey, though they did not measure directly whether prey was more plentiful there. The findings point to the value of remaining natural vegetation, but they do not suggest that every king cobra uses farmland in the same way.How do roads and villages affect king cobra movementRoads and human settlements can expose king cobras to threats such as vehicle collisions and conflict with people. Even so, the researchers found no consistent evidence that the snakes avoided them. The animals kept using available habitat patches, even close to roads or settlements. The study also recorded that the snakes spent an average of 2.3 days at shelter sites and returned to places they had used before roughly every 13 days. The researchers found no consistent link between distance to landscape features and either the time snakes spent at shelter sites or how often they went back. They also reported wide variation in how long individual snakes spent in human-disturbed areas. Across the tracked animals, it ranged from 0.7 per cent to 100 per cent of the tracking period, which underlines how differently individual king cobras used the landscape.How can forest corridors and irrigation canals protect king cobrasThe researchers concluded that irrigation canals and forest fragments may help king cobras persist in agricultural areas cut off from protected forests. They said future conservation research should focus on how these links are kept in place and how threats to the snakes can be reduced. The paper also suggested that road-crossing structures combined with fencing could help with the danger roads pose.The study stressed that king cobras are vulnerable outside protected areas, where they can face direct and indirect human-caused mortality. The researchers also pointed to the need to reduce persecution of the snakes and improve humane snake-removal services. They cautioned that their findings rest on a small sample of seven individuals, whose movement patterns differed. The results cannot be assumed to represent all king cobra populations across their range.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Google founder Larry Page publicly announced that he will give his billions to Elon Musk, but how an 'argument' over AI changed their friendship forever …
articles.summary: Google co-founder Larry Page once said he would consider leaving his entire fortune to Elon Musk rather than giving it to a traditional charity.
articles.body: Google co-founder Larry Page once said he would consider leaving his entire fortune to Elon Musk rather than giving it to a traditional charity. The two billionaires were once close friends who shared a vision of changing humanity's future. But years later, their relationship reportedly cooled over disagreements about artificial intelligence (AI) and the risks it could pose to humanity. Larry Page's unusual idea of giving his wealth to Musk came into the spotlight during a 2014 TED interview with Charlie Rose. The interviewer reminded Page of an earlier statement in which the Google co-founder had expressed confidence in Musk's ability to shape the future."You once said ... that you might consider, rather than giving your money to a cause, simply giving it to Elon Musk because you had confidence he would change the future," Rose said.Larry Page agreed with the idea, explaining that Musk's ambition to make humanity a multiplanetary species was itself a form of philanthropy. "He wants to go to Mars — to back up humanity. That's a company, and it's philanthropical. So I think we aim to do kind of similar things," Page said.Why Larry Page wanted to leave his fortune to Elon MuskThe idea was not just an offhand remark during the TED interview. It had reportedly come up a year earlier at a Stanford event in 2013. During an interview with Elon Musk at the ENCORE Award event, venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson recalled a conversation at a Google lunch where Page unexpectedly spoke about his wealth and what would happen to it if he died.Jurvetson said Larry Page had remarked, "If I got hit by a bus today, I should leave all of it to Elon Musk." The audience laughed at the statement. Elon Musk, who appeared surprised, asked whether Page had really said that before smiling and referring to him as a good friend.How AI disagreement reportedly changed Elon Musk and Larry Page’s friendshipThe two entrepreneurs had known each other long before they became some of the world's richest technology leaders. Musk had met Page before securing venture funding for his companies, and their friendship grew around conversations about artificial intelligence, space exploration and the future of humanity.For Larry Page, Musk's plans to build a future beyond Earth appeared to align with his own belief that technology could help solve some of humanity's biggest challenges.Despite their shared interests, the relationship between Page and Musk reportedly became strained over artificial intelligence. Both men had strong views about the technology, but their perspectives on its long-term risks differed. Musk has repeatedly warned about the dangers of advanced AI and the need for safeguards. Page, meanwhile, has been associated with a more optimistic view of technological progress. Reports have suggested that their disagreement over AI contributed to the cooling of their friendship.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong jailed for 10 more years
articles.summary: Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Thursday after being convicted for a second time under
articles.body: Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Thursday after being convicted for a second time under Beijing-imposed national security legislation. The case has drawn criticism from observers who view it as another example of the authorities' crackdown on the city's once-vibrant pro-democracy movement.Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiring to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the legislation. He pleaded guilty to the charge in September, a step that can generally lead to a reduced sentence.The 30-year-old activist is already serving a four-year-and-eight-month prison term in connection with Hong Kong's largest national security case, which stemmed from an unofficial primary election. He had earlier been expected to complete that sentence and walk free in January 2027 before facing the latest prosecution.During Thursday's sentencing hearing, Judge William Tam described Wong's offence as particularly serious and rejected arguments that his involvement had been limited.The judge said he had initially considered a 13-year prison term but reduced the sentence in view of Wong's guilty plea.Wong appeared composed as he thanked his supporters before leaving the courtroom. Those gathered outside waved to him, while Tiffany Chin, a former member of scholarism, the student group once led by Wong, was seen in tears.The judge also ruled that Wong's two prison sentences could run concurrently. The activist has approximately two months remaining on his earlier sentence for the previous national security conviction.Resident ET Wong recalled that Joshua Wong had demonstrated exceptional political awareness even as a teenager, possessing what she described as a level of "big-picture thinking" that many adults lacked. She said he had taken a difficult path while fighting for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement."At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment," she said.Wong's convictions seen as a warning against dissentHong Kong was once known for its active civil society, extensive protest movements and vibrant media landscape. However, following the anti-government demonstrations that swept the city in 2019, authorities introduced changes that limited electoral choices and arrested several prominent activists.Several media organisations known for their critical coverage of the government subsequently shut down, while dozens of civil society groups also disbanded.Observers believe Wong's latest sentence demonstrates the authorities' determination to keep high-profile activists behind bars for extended periods, potentially discouraging further civic and political activism."NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Asian Law, referring to the National Security Law.Beijing, however, considers Wong an anti-China figure who supports Hong Kong independence, a position that crosses its political red lines. Hong Kong authorities have defended the security legislation, arguing that it is essential to maintaining stability following the 2019 unrest. They have also maintained that law enforcement measures are based on evidence.Prosecution focuses on international lobbying effortsDuring the proceedings, prosecutors alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed around 2016 to pursue international lobbying efforts to advance their campaign for democratic self-determination.The prosecution claimed that, even before the national security legislation was introduced, the two activists had called for sanctions and other punitive measures against Hong Kong and mainland China.It cited Wong's meetings with American politicians, including Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio, in 2016 and 2019 as part of the evidence presented against him.According to prosecutors, after the security law came into force, Law and other activists continued their international advocacy by meeting foreign political leaders and organising petition campaigns.Wong allegedly supported these efforts from Hong Kong through interviews with international media organisations and social media campaigns. Prosecutors said his activities were aimed at attracting foreign governments' attention and strengthening demands for sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong.Earlier, Wong's lawyer, Derek Chan, had urged the court to consider a sentence that would allow his client to retain some hope for the future. He also told the court that Wong hoped to look after his parents following his release.Friends have said that during nearly six years behind bars, Wong continued reading books, exercising and learning to play the guitar on his own. articles.title: Nine people set off on a one-hour boat trip between islands in Micronesia on July 30, but a storm swept them away; about three months and 5,400 km later, villagers on a Kiribati island rescued five of them
articles.summary: A routine boat journey between two islands in the Federated States of Micronesia turned into a months-long ordeal after a storm swept nine people off
articles.body: A routine boat journey between two islands in the Federated States of Micronesia turned into a months-long ordeal after a storm swept nine people off course in the Pacific Ocean. Nearly three months after they disappeared, five of them, including two children, were found alive by villagers on a remote island in Kiribati, around 5,400 kilometres from where their journey began.The group had set off on July 30 aboard a 20-foot skiff for what was expected to be a one-hour crossing between Murilo and Ruo, two islands in the Hall Islands of Micronesia's Chuuk state. But the boat failed to return to Ruo as scheduled, triggering a search operation that continued for 10 days before authorities suspended it in August.The five survivors were eventually spotted near Fanning Island, also known as Tabuaeran, in Kiribati on Sunday, November 1. Their rescue brought relief to families who had spent months without news of the missing boat, although the fate of the other four passengers remains unknown, according to reports by ABC News Australia.A one-hour crossing that turned into a vast search operationThe US Coast Guard's Joint Rescue Sub-Center in Guam received notification at around 10 am on July 31 that the skiff, carrying nine people, had not returned to Ruo Island the previous day. The Coast Guard coordinated with local and international partners, issued maritime safety broadcasts and mobilised available search resources.According to its August 10 statement, the 10-day operation covered approximately 25,000 square nautical miles and involved more than 31 search patterns. The search included a US Coast Guard cutter and aircraft, US Air Force and Navy aircraft, a vessel from the Federated States of Micronesia, and two commercial ships that volunteered to assist.Despite the extensive effort, rescuers found no trace of the boat or its passengers. The Coast Guard suspended its active search on August 9, saying it had made a difficult decision after the operation. The boat's disappearance had left families waiting for news, with little indication of where the small vessel might have been carried by the open ocean.Villagers spot the boat thousands of kilometres awayThe breakthrough came on November 1, when residents of Fanning Island spotted the drifting boat off the remote Kiribati island and rescued the five people aboard. The group had travelled an estimated 5,400 kilometres east from the Federated States of Micronesia. The survivors were identified by ABC as Wanis Weita, Wboy Weita, Akinis David, Paul Paul and Tedwin Paul. They included three adults and two children.Kiribati MP Kaotitaake Rakoroa told ABC that the survivors were taken in and cared for by the pastor of the local Uniting Church. Medical officials on the island also examined them after their rescue. Rakoroa said police on nearby Kiritimati Island had relayed news of the discovery to him in the capital, Tarawa.The survivors were reportedly in a serious physical condition after spending so long at sea. Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told ABC that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were given intravenous fluids and began showing signs of recovery. "They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," Tororo told the broadcaster, describing the improvement in their condition. The survivors have not spoken publicly about what happened during the months they were adrift and have asked for their privacy to be respected.Four passengers remain unaccounted forWhile the rescue has reunited five people with the possibility of returning home, it has not resolved the fate of everyone who boarded the boat in July. Chuuk State Governor Alexander Narruhn acknowledged the rescue in a statement, saying nine people had been aboard the missing vessel and expressing gratitude that five had been found. He also said authorities continued to pray for the other four."There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine people have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter, according to the Associated Press.The US Coast Guard also welcomed the discovery. In a statement to AP, it described the news as "incredible and wonderful" and said it was glad the five survivors had been found and were receiving care. It also expressed condolences to the families and friends of those who had not arrived with them.Authorities have not confirmed what happened to the four missing passengers. Narruhn said he had begun discussions with the Kiribati government to arrange the survivors' return to Micronesia.
